name: Cornwall/Kernow
text: Cornwall/Kernow is the southwesternmost part of Britain, long a home of the Brythonic Celtic language Cornish. Kernow is simply the Cornish name for Cornwall. Around 1100 the tongue ran from the river Tamar to Land's End, and close to twenty thousand of the county's roughly twenty-one thousand people spoke it. The centuries after saw Cornish give ground, retreating westwards until only the far west kept it alive into the early modern period. MacKillop's Dictionary records that the last native speaker of Cornish died during the 1700s. By about 1800 the language was almost gone. Revivalists then worked to bring it back, and modern Cornish still tends to reflect English phonetics. They urge a stress on the penultimate syllable, as in Welsh, and today the tongue is once more taught and spoken. Scholars such as Henry Jenner, R. Morton Nance, and others led the late nineteenth-century revival. A new institutional chapter came in 1927 with the founding of the Gorseth Kernow, the Cornish gorsedd, a gathering modelled on the Welsh institution that celebrates poetry, music, and culture. Its appearance in that year placed Cornwall in a family of revivals that also produced a Breton gorsedd in 1901. The Cornish also keep a strong emblem, the chough, a bird tied to the county's identity and named with the definite article as a local mark. It represents a pride in the culture that endured through the long decline of the language.
